title: Dolly Parton to Be Celebrated at L.A. Tribute Concert Featuring Instrumental Renditions of ‘Jolene,’ ‘9 to 5’ and ‘I Will Always Love You’

body:

	Just two months after Dolly Parton’s death, fans will have another opportunity to celebrate the country music legend’s extraordinary catalog.

	Fever’s popular Candlelight concert series is bringing a tribute to Parton to the Ritz-Carlton in Marina del Rey on Oct. 30, featuring classical arrangements of some of her best-known songs performed by a live string quartet. Fever is also putting an another tribute concert at the Los Angeles Equestrian Center on Dec. 4.


	The concert comes amid an outpouring of tributes to the Grammy-winning singer, who died Aug. 25 following a brief battle with cancer. The hour-long performance will revisit her legacy through instrumental renditions of songs including “Jolene,” “Coat of Many Colors,” “9 to 5” and “I Will Always Love You,” the latter of which became an even bigger pop phenomenon after Whitney Houston recorded it for 1992’s “The Bodyguard.”

	Orchid Quartet will lead the evening’s performance, with a tentative 15-song setlist that also includes “Islands in the Stream,” Parton’s chart-topping duet with Kenny Rogers; “Wildflowers,” which she recorded alongside Linda Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris for their 1987 album “Trio”; and early-career selections such as “Dumb Blonde” and “Just Because I’m a Woman.” Other songs on the program include “Here You Come Again,” “Two Doors Down,” “My Tennessee Mountain Home” and “Light of a Clear Blue Morning.”

	The performance will take place in the Ritz-Carlton’s grand ballroom, where hundreds of flickering electric candles will surround the musicians. The intimate setting is a departure from the elaborate costumes, rhinestones and larger-than-life stage productions for which Parton’s live performances became known.


	The Los Angeles concert arrives amid a wave of musical tributes to Parton. Over the weekend, Miley Cyrus honored her late godmother during an emotional performance at the Hollywood Bowl, where she performed “Jolene” and reflected on their decades-long relationship. The singer has been among the many artists celebrating Parton’s influence since her death, which prompted tributes from across the music and entertainment industries.

	Fever’s Candlelight series has built a global business around reimagining familiar catalogs through classical instrumentation, with previous programs celebrating everyone from the Beatles and Fleetwood Mac to Adele, Taylor Swift and Hans Zimmer. The concerts are typically staged in unconventional venues, including historic churches, museums and luxury hotels. 

	Unlike an official estate production, the Dolly Parton concert is an independently organized tribute and is not affiliated with or endorsed by the singer’s estate.

	Tickets are available now through Fever.

schema.headline: Dolly Parton to Be Celebrated at L.A. Tribute Concert Featuring Instrumental Renditions of ‘Jolene,’ ‘9 to 5’ and ‘I Will Always Love You’

	First came the laptop harness from “The Rehearsal.” Now it’s a pair of $8 headphones from “You Can See Everything.” Once again, Nathan Fielder has become an unlikely source of affordable Halloween costume inspiration, this time courtesy of his buzzy Elizabeth Holmes documentary.

	The comedian and filmmaker’s latest accessory — a pair of black, foam-padded headphones he wears while investigating the disgraced Theranos founder — is now making the rounds online. Internet sleuths have identified them as HamiltonBuhl SchoolMate headphones, which retail for just $7.99.



	The new costume inspiration comes courtesy of “You Can See Everything,” the A24 documentary Fielder co-directed with Lance Oppenheim, which opened in theaters Oct. 16 following a surprise premiere at the Telluride Film Festival.

	The nearly three-hour film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes during the final 34 days before she began serving her prison sentence in 2023. Fielder and Oppenheim embed themselves in Holmes’ domestic life alongside her partner, Billy Evans, and their children, offering an unusually intimate portrait of the former Silicon Valley entrepreneur before her incarceration.

	For a niche couples costume, the jailed tech founder also has an equally recognizable uniform: a black turtleneck, black trousers, a slicked-back blonde ponytail and her signature red lipstick. Add a Theranos-branded badge or a prop blood-testing device for good measure. The Steve Jobs-inspired ensemble has been a Halloween favorite since Holmes’ spectacular fall from grace, and most of the pieces are easy to find on Amazon or in your own closet.

title: Collage, a New Management and Investment Company, Launches as a Bridge Between AI-First Studios and Hollywood (EXCLUSIVE)
description: As Hollywood continues to navigate the plethora of questions surrounding AI and its place in the industry, one former talent agent hopes to be the
body:
As Hollywood continues to navigate the plethora of questions surrounding AI and its place in the industry, one former talent agent hopes to be the link between everyone involved.

	Enter Collage, a new management and investment company aimed at helping AI-first production companies navigate the Hollywood pipeline. Founded in July by former UTA agent Dante DeSario and media investor Michael Lambert, who worked within the talent agency’s independent film group before leaving in March, the company has completed a seed funding round — the amount of which DeSario would not disclose — backed by a suite of investors and advisers: Black Bear and Fundamental Films, Dennis Miller, Blue Deer Media, GOAL Ventures, AGC Studios, Roy Lee, Marty Bowen, Todd Lieberman, Todd Garner, Barry Porter, George Huber, Max Michael and Ric Roman Waugh, among others. The firm, based in Beverly Hills, currently has five full-time employees and roughly a dozen part-time staffers.
	

	The earliest inklings for Collage came in February 2024, after DeSario got his hands on an early demo of OpenAI’s short-lived video generator Sora. After meeting with — and signing — some filmmakers who played with the generator and seeing them build their own companies focused on AI productions, DeSario realized that his own venture could “support these artists in a way that they needed help in various degrees” while helping “Hollywood navigate this, frankly, incredibly sensitive time over AI.”


	Much of DeSario’s work includes aiding the initial batch of companies — which includes AI studios like Asteria, Native Foreign, Obsidian, and Jason Zada’s Secret Level — as they navigate Hollywood guilds, “studio bureaucrats,” copyright issues and demonstrations of the technology’s capabilities. DeSario’s firm also acts as an investment company, though he would not disclose which companies he’s invested in. “We’re here to offer the menu of things to what this new category needs,” he says.
	

	On the Hollywood side, DeSario wants to demonstrate to studios which companies are making human-led work and “who to stay away from” in an era of seemingly never-ending upstarts.

	Collage’s model comes as legacy Hollywood companies figure out how to engage with AI at a time when consternation persists among both creatives and audiences over issues surrounding jobs, slop content and the impact on creativity. DeSario hopes Collage can act as “infrastructure,” a bridge between the various stakeholders in the industry that allows more stories to be told while encouraging acceptance of the technology.

	“I’m an independent film guy,” he said. “I just want to help filmmakers get their projects made. That was my whole intention, and realizing that this is something that is unlike what a lot of people think. There’s a lot of fallacy. It’s not pushing a button. There’s real craft and real differentiation between those who can have taste and want to tell stories and helping them get out there.”

	He’s also hoping that, as more of these companies emerge, they’ll be able to compete with and complement the companies that have maintained footprints in Hollywood through their traditional filmmaking offerings. “The legacy system should be inviting them because they’re incredible craftspeople to work with all of the various people who are already working on films,” DeSario says.

	A goal for him, he says, is to help audiences witness the AI version of a “Toy Story” moment, or a film developed with AI that breaks through with general moviegoers.

	“I’ve personally seen work that has made me feel something,” he says. “You want to feel something. I’ve had that experience. I think a lot of people haven’t had that experience, and because it’s hard to feel something when there’s so much fear in the air. I want to help show the general audiences and help facilitate what I’ve seen to everyone else because it’s pretty potent.”

title: Maeve Communications Launches New York-Based Communications Company (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Maeve Communications, co-founded by industry veterans Laura Puig and Michelle Ciciyasvili, announced Monday the launch of its new publicity and str
body:
Maeve Communications, co-founded by industry veterans Laura Puig and Michelle Ciciyasvili, announced Monday the launch of its new publicity and strategic communications company.

	The New York-based company will focus on entertainment, media and talent services offering project-based consultation and executive coaching services.

	“The conversation to start our own company began in 2019 while working together briefly at a PR agency, but we knew we needed more experience before confidently building something of our own,” co-founders Puig and Ciciyasvili said in a joint statement. “The time for Maeve Communications is now. In merging our complementary backgrounds and experience, we’re ready and eager to partner with our clients and deliver thoughtful strategy, creative ideas, and the straightforward counsel they deserve. We take our work seriously but believe in having some fun, keeping things real and breaking a few rules along the way.”
	

	Puig recently left Tubi to launch her own publicity and strategic communications company with business partner Ciciyasvili, who was most recently the senior director of comms at Betches. Puig is an experienced publicist with a history of clients across television, film, talent, creator and entertainment industries. Throughout her 13 years of experience, she has developed long-standing press relationships, and garnered media hits across broadcast, print, online, podcast, digital and radio.


	Michelle Ciciyasvili is a communications leader with 15 years of public relations experience across media, entertainment, lifestyle and fashion brands. She blends creative storytelling and strategic thinking with her knowledge of how entertainment, media and culture intersect with business.
	

	Maeve is inspired by Hollywood legend Mae West who was an American actress, singer, comedian, screenwriter and playwright in the 1930s. The founders said West serves as a symbol of the company’s “no-nonsense approach” when providing direct, senior-level counsel on the basis of honest and targeted conversations for each client.

schema.headline: Maeve Communications Launches New York-Based Communications Company (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Agents and Indie Producers Argue Incentives Alone Won’t Fix Hollywood’s Ills
description: It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cu
body:
It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cutting-edge TV.

	The FCC’s “financial interest and syndication” rules forced TV networks to buy shows from superproducers like Norman Lear and Grant Tinker rather than making them in-house. And ever since the FCC did away with fin-syn 30 years ago, producers and agents have been longing for its return.
	

	Now, with momentum building behind a U.S. film incentive, they are hoping the moment is ripe to recreate fin-syn for the streaming era. They argue it would bring a jolt of creativity and a spirit of enterprise to a business stuck in a creative slump. 


	The major agencies — WME, CAA and UTA — announced last week that they are forming a coalition with production companies including Imagine Entertainment and Legendary to push for legislation that would force streamers to buy at least 50% of their original content from independent producers. The legislation would also limit the length of licensing terms, reviving secondary markets that have largely withered away.

	Their message is that Hollywood ails not only from runaway production, but also from a consolidated ecosystem that limits creativity and makes it harder for producers, writers and actors to profit from their labor.

	“The tax incentive may change where the production shoots, but it doesn’t change who owns and profits from it,” argued Ken Ziffren, co-founder of Ziffren Brittenham LLP, who has been campaigning for a restoration of fin-syn for decades. “We think the tax legislation only goes so far to help our industry and it’s not a complete effort, and it can’t be a complete effort, unless it’s paired with a modernized ownership framework.”
	

	Jeff Sagansky, a producer, investor and longtime fin-syn supporter, argued that overseas incentives are not the only reason that U.S. production jobs are going away.

	“They’re also going away because of the way the streaming business has consolidated around four players,” he said. “They act as an oligopoly. They’ve got incredible pricing power,” saying the streamers are ordering 30-40% fewer hours of programming than they were a few years ago.

	Getting the idea through Congress will be an uphill battle, and will face adamant opposition from Netflix, Amazon and the other streaming platforms. The effort also has the potential to sow division within an industry that has united behind the goal of passing the first-ever federal film incentive.

	Supporters wanted to some version of their ideas into the tax credit bill that was introduced to much fanfare in September. But while they had some positive meetings, they were ultimately rebuffed. They are now aiming for 2027, when Democrats are expected to take control of at least one of the houses of Congress.

	Rep. Laura Friedman, a co-author of the tax incentive as well as a former producer, said in a statement that she sympathizes with producers’ concerns about industry consolidation and the threat to diverse voices in entertainment.

	“My focus right now is on passing our bipartisan national film tax credit bill to put film and television workers back on the job, but I look forward to continuing to work with stakeholders to ensure the industry is vibrant for the future,” she said.

	The Streaming Innovation Alliance, which includes Netflix and other streamers, issued a statement on Thursday calling the proposal a package of “blunt government mandates” that would “only dampen production and discourage creative risk-taking.”

	The Federal Communications Commission adopted the fin-syn rules in 1970, when there were only three TV networks. The rules prevented networks from owning syndication rights in their shows, and later, from owning shows that aired in primetime. The rules are credited with leading to an era of groundbreaking TV, including “All in the Family,” “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and “The Cosby Show.”

	The repeal of the rules in the mid-90s spurred a wave of vertical integration, as Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC and Viacom acquired CBS.
	

	Arguing that the end of fin-syn had killed off independent production, a group called the Coalition for Program Diversity urged the FCC to reinstate a version of it. In 2002, the coalition — led by Ziffren — sought a new regulation that 25% of primetime programming come from independent producers. In a deregulatory era, such pleas fell on deaf ears.

	Nowadays, streamers typically either make shows themselves or buy from the handful of other major studios. When they do buy from indie producers, they typically take all rights for 10-20 years, locking the producers out of the option of selling into secondary markets.

	Mark Vahradian, producer of the “Transformers” franchise and other films, argued that streamers are so powerful that they can dictate those terms, and that dynamic ultimately hurts consumers.

	“There’s no incentive for the creators to go out and build something brand new,” said Vahradian, a founding member of Producers United. “That’s why they’re only making sequels and franchise titles. They own those and have no motivation to say ‘Why don’t we do something new?’”

	For years there wasn’t much opportunity to do anything about it. But with President Trump vowing to “save” Hollywood from a dramatic downturn, fin-syn supporters see an opening.

	The initiative would require an act of Congress, as the FCC’s ambit is limited to the public airwaves.

	Andrew Long, a senior fellow at the Free State Foundation, a free-market think tank, argued that the streaming marketplace is far more diversified now than the three-network era of the 1970s.

	“It’s hard to find factual predicate that would justify this kind of government intervention in the video distribution marketplace in 2026,” Long said, adding that it could raise First Amendment concerns. “I think there would be high scrutiny, and I think that given the state of the marketplace and the options available, it might not pass muster.”

	But Rich Shuter, head of business affairs at UTA, argued that consolidation leaves his agency’s clients without much leverage — and viewers without much choice.

	“We’re going back to a situation where you have these streaming conglomerates controlling all the content the country is viewing,” Shuter said. “They’re determining what is being produced.”
	

	Shuter said that more risk-taking will lead to a more vibrant ecosystem.

	“We don’t want to stall the federal tax credit from being passed as quickly as possible,” he said. “We hope the administration and Congress recognize this is a supplemental benefit.”

schema.headline: Agents and Indie Producers Argue Incentives Alone Won’t Fix Hollywood’s Ills

title: Banijay CEO Marco Bassetti Urges European Producers to Fight for Better Terms of Trade With Hollywood: Studios and Streamers Should Provide ‘Rewards for Creativity’
description: Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, called for European producers to hold their grou
body:
Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, called for European producers to hold their ground when it comes to negotiating terms of trade with the U.S. studios and streamers during a fireside chat at Rome’s MIA market titled “What does it mean today to be a ‘European champion’ in an increasingly competitive global content market?”

	“Who invests in creativity? It’s us independent producers,” said Bassetti during the chat with veteran Italian producer Marco Chimenz. He went on to point out that “the major debate currently taking place in Europe — and this is my own personal view — regardless of the different legal systems, across different countries we live under, is about recognizing and providing compensation for creativity,” he added.
	

	The Italian executive went on to point out that “the current battle [in Brussels] over [investment] quotas is instead entirely pointless.” He was referring to contentious rules – known as Europe’s Audiovisual Media Services Directive – that force foreign streaming services to invest a portion of their revenue into local productions, but leaves the modalities of this obligation to each individual country.


	But Bassetti sees the rules of engagement as being crucial.

	“The real fight should focus on studios and streamers recognizing and providing rewards for creativity” in the form of retention of IP rights on the part of producers, Bassetti added. “Yet that is not what is happening.” 

	At least not in continental Europe. “But when I work for a TV network — especially in countries like England — I retain ownership of the intellectual property,” he noted. “If I sell a series, the rights eventually revert to me after three years and there’s a built-in incentive for the creator.”
	

	“Here in Europe, we’re accustomed to a system like that,” Bassetti said. “If the streamers just treat production companies as mere service providers it’s a problem,” because you don’t provide an incentive for creators to work with you. 

	“The reality is that we have no ownership, and it’s extremely difficult to secure any, though things are starting to open up a bit. There’s some movement regarding ‘windows’ (the sequence of release platforms)—but it’s only a partial shift. Ultimately, they [the studios and the streamers] still have total control,” he said.

	Since taking the helm of Stéphane Courbit’s media powerhouse Banijay in 2013, Bassetti has firmly steered the company through some major transformations, from the takeover of production powerhouse Endemol Shine in the thick of the pandemic in 2020 to the diversification of the banner’s activities in live entertainment through Balich Wonder Studio and the Independents, all the while ramping up both scripted and unscripted business, and bolstering new and existing IPs.

	It was only two months ago that Banijay Entertainment and RedBird IMI officially completed the $8 billion merger of Banijay and RedBird IMI’s All3Media, which is headquartered in London, U.K. The deal saw All3Media CEO Jane Turton take on the role of deputy CEO of the combined company, which boasts over 265,000 hours of content and some of television’s most recognizable franchises.

	While the company is best known for its unscripted IP, thanks to “super brands” like “The Traitors,” “Big Brother” and “MasterChef,”  Banijay also makes plenty of top notch  scripted TV series and movies such as “Peaky Blinders,” “Black Mirror” and “Hamnet.” 

	Last week, speaking at the Mipcom TV market in Cannes, Bassetti said he saw an opportunity for the company to grow its presence in scripted production and hinted to an expansion into the U.S. scripted space.

	That might help improve terms of trade for Banijay.

title: Laurene Powell Jobs Invested $250 Million in David Ellison’s Skydance
description: Billionaire and philanthropist Laurene Powell Jobs paid $250 million to acquire a stake in Skydance, the David Ellison-led company formed by the me
body:
Billionaire and philanthropist Laurene Powell Jobs paid $250 million to acquire a stake in Skydance, the David Ellison-led company formed by the merger of Paramount Skydance and Warner Bros. Discovery.

	Powell Jobs, founder and president of Emerson Collective, was named to the board of Skydance on Oct. 5 alongside former Activision chief Bobby Kotick, which was announced the following day.


	With her board appointment, Powell Jobs acquired 20.83 million shares of Skydance Corp. for $12 each, for a total of $250 million. She indirectly owns those shares, which are held in a trust, per an SEC filing disclosing the investment.
	

	In addition to that investment, Powell Jobs — in her capacity as a Skydance board member — was granted 33,118 restricted stock units in the company. Those are scheduled to vest with Skydance’s 2027 annual meeting of stockholders.

	At Emerson Collective, which she launched in 2011, Powell Jobs has “paired philanthropy with venture capital investing to support entrepreneurs tackling complex global challenges,” according to her official bio. “She believes that investing in education, economic mobility, immigration, and energy can expand opportunity for the next generation and that high-quality independent journalism is essential to a functioning democracy.”

	Through Emerson Collective, Powell Jobs is the lead investor of Anonymous Content, an independent production and management company, and Concordia Studio, which describes itself as a “talent-first” film and television studio, founded by filmmaker Davis Guggenheim. She is the majority investor and chair of the board of the Atlantic under a deal reached in 2017. Emerson Collective also has invested in artificial intelligence giants OpenAI and Anthropic. Powell Jobs, who was married to late Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, has a current net worth estimated at $15.8 billion, according to Forbes.
	

	Skydance brings together two major Hollywood studios, streamers HBO Max and Paramount+, and TV networks including CBS, CNN, Comedy Central, MTV, Nickelodeon, TBS and TNT.

	The Ellison family — with the multibillion-dollar backing of Larry Ellison, David’s tech-mogul father — holds the largest equity stake in Skydance. RedBird Capital Partners, led by managing partner Gerry Cardinale, invested $4 billion into Skydance. Equity investors in the Paramount-WBD merger also included the sovereign wealth funds of Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Abu Dhabi. The Ellisons and investment firm RedBird Capital Partners together are the sole holders of Paramount Class A common stock, including 100% of the combined company’s voting shares.

	Skydance, in announcing her appointment to the board, said it “believes that Ms. Powell Jobs is qualified to serve as a member of the board because of her extensive experience and focus investing in innovative and entrepreneurial enterprises and on high-quality journalism.”

	Powell Jobs also co-founded and serves on the boards of the Waverley Street Foundation, College Track and the XQ Institute, aimed at advancing community-led climate solutions and strengthening educational outcomes. In addition, she serves on the boards of Chicago CRED and the Ford Foundation. She is a member of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences and a recipient of the Stanford Graduate School of Business’s Ernest C. Arbuckle Award for excellence in the field of management leadership.

schema.headline: Laurene Powell Jobs Invested $250 Million in David Ellison’s Skydance

	Fagbenle (“The Handmaid’s Tale,” “Presumed Innocent”) plays Hayes. He is repped by Buchwald, Artists First and Hansen, Jacobson, Teller, Hoberman, Newman, Warren, Richman, Rush, Kaller, Gellman, Meigs & Fox.

title: Sony Pictures Television Hires Lauren Glaubach, Former YouTube and Pinterest Exec, to Lead Digital and Social Distribution Strategy
description: Sony Pictures Television hired Lauren Glaubach, a former YouTube and Pinterest content exec, in the newly created role of executive vice president,
body:
Sony Pictures Television hired Lauren Glaubach, a former YouTube and Pinterest content exec, in the newly created role of executive vice president, distribution, digital and social platforms. 

	Glaubach will head up Sony Pictures Entertainment’s continued expansion across YouTube and other digital platforms, reporting to Jason Spivak and Paul Littmann, presidents of distribution and networks at SPT. She’s tasked with unlocking “new opportunities” for the company’s film and television library and “maximizing” the value of its IP, Sony Pictures Television said.
	

	Glaubach joins the company as Sony Pictures Television has stepped up efforts to boost revenue from digital platforms. Recent initiatives include the announcement of “Jeopardy! YouTube Edition Volume 2”; the launch of “Reading Rainbow” on YouTube; and a newly announced partnership with Prof. Brian Cox, a professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester, to develop premium original content for digital audiences.


	“Lauren has spent her career working at the intersection of content, platforms, and audiences, and has a proven track record of building and growing digital businesses,” Spivak and Littmann said in a joint statement. “We’re very pleased to have her join SPT and are excited about what we can accomplish together.”

	Glaubach most recently was at Pinterest, where she served as VP, head of global content partnerships, leading a team responsible for overseeing the platform’s content producer network and creator communities. Prior to Pinterest, she spent more than a decade at YouTube in senior strategy, programming, partnerships and operations roles, most recently serving as director, global head of kids and family content partnerships and programming. During her tenure at YouTube, Glaubach managed a partner portfolio of more than 500 channels spanning traditional media and YouTube-first creators.
	

	Earlier in her career, Glaubach held strategy, brand management and marketing roles at Disney and BloomSpot, an e-commerce marketplace. She earned a bachelor or arts degree in psychology from Princeton University and an MBA from Harvard Business School.

	Glaubach, in a statement provided by SPT, said: “The ways audiences engage with entertainment continue to evolve, creating meaningful opportunities to extend the reach and impact of the stories and franchises they love. I’m excited to join Sony Pictures and work with this talented team to develop digital experiences that meet audiences where they are, deepen their connection to our content, and open up new possibilities for our iconic brands.”

schema.headline: Sony Pictures Television Hires Lauren Glaubach, Former YouTube and Pinterest Exec, to Lead Digital and Social Distribution Strategy

title: ‘Running Point’ Co-Creator Mindy Kaling Joins Season 3 Cast
description:
Mindy Kaling, writer, executive producer and co-creator of “Running Point,” has picked up one more title on the Netflix show: star.

	Kaling is ste
body:
Mindy Kaling, writer, executive producer and co-creator of “Running Point,” has picked up one more title on the Netflix show: star.

	Kaling is stepping in front of the cameras for Season 3 in the recurring role of Divya, an outspoken, confident CEO of a popular gambling app. Per the character description, “Much like Isla (Kate Hudson), she’s proudly the first female leader in her male dominated field. Their similarities end there with Divya becoming a thorn in Isla’s plans all season.”
	

	Production on “Running Point” Season 3 is underway in Los Angeles. Kate Hudson will direct the first episode, marking her television directorial debut. Returning cast includes Drew Tarver, Scott MacArthur, Brenda Song, Fabrizio Guido, Chet Hanks, Toby Sandeman and Justin Theroux, with recurring actors Ray Romano, Uche Agada, Ken Marino and Jay Ellis.


	“Running Point” follows Isla (Hudson), a former party girl and college dropout who is unexpectedly left in charge of her family’s pro basketball team. In Season 2, she is “no longer the surprise choice to lead the Los Angeles Waves, she’s the one everyone is watching,” per the logline. “With the franchise finally rebounding after last year’s scandal, Isla is determined to prove she’s not just keeping the seat warm for her brother Cam (Justin Theroux). What she doesn’t know is that Cam is quietly maneuvering behind the scenes to reclaim his post, turning every misstep into ammunition. As she tries to balance the pressure of running a franchise with devoting time to her personal life, every decision on and off the court counts. To survive the family power plays and the scrutiny of the board, she’ll have to rip up last season’s game plan and come up with a whole new playbook if she wants to close out the season on top.”
	

	The sports comedy series hails from writers and executive producers Kaling, David Stassen (who also showruns) and Ike Barinholtz. Hudson, Howard Klein, Jeanie Buss and Linda Rambis also serve as EPs. The series is produced by Mindy Kaling’s Kaling International in association with Warner Bros. Television. Kaling and Stassen are both under overall deals with WBTV.

schema.headline: ‘Running Point’ Co-Creator Mindy Kaling Joins Season 3 Cast

            Richard Riehle -- famous for his role as Tom Smykowski in "Office Space" -- is dead ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Friends of Richard tell TMZ ... he died of natural causes last Thursday in Los Angeles.
      
    
            He was an acclaimed character actor, appearing in over 400 projects during a long career in Hollywood.
      

            Richard's best known for his work in "Office Space" ... he plays Tom, the product manager who gets laid off from Initech, survives a hit-and-run accident, and lands a massive financial settlement that allows him to follow his dreams and build his prototype "Jump to Conclusions" mat. He's got tons of memorable scenes and lines, and is a cult favorite.
      
    
        
                    
                      MAY 2018
                  
      
    
            The last time we caught up with Richard was back in 2018 in Los Angeles, after he had just gotten back from filming the Lifetime holiday movie "A Very Nutty Christmas" with Melissa Joan Hart.
      
    
            Richard was 78.
      
    
            RIP

            Sahara Ray, the Australian model and swimwear designer who once made headlines for her relationship with Justin Bieber, has died ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            "She passed away last night surrounded by family at the hospital. She was so loved," Sahara's family tells TMZ.
      
    
            Her cause of death has not been confirmed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Ray rose to fame through her modeling career and social media presence, building a massive following on Instagram while launching her own swimwear brand, Sahara Ray Swim.
      

            She made headlines in 2016 when she was photographed vacationing with Bieber in Hawaii. She was also previously romantically linked to Australian singer Cody Simpson.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The model was the daughter of legendary Australian surfer Tony Ray and spent much of her childhood traveling between Australia, California and Hawaii.
      
    
            In 2024, Sahara opened up about her battle with Guillain-Barré syndrome -- a rare neurological disorder that left her partially paralyzed following a serious car accident.
      
    
            She was 34.
      
    
            RIP
